subject: chemistry
title: Identification of common gases
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Identification of common gases — AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification, section 4.8.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry (AQA) practice covering Identification of common gases, specification section 4.8.2.
final_note: You worked through Identification of common gases — 4 specification statements.

concepts.def: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of the gas. A positive result is that the gas burns rapidly with a pop sound.
A wooden splint that has been lit and is still alight. In the hydrogen test it is held at the open end of the test tube, not pushed down into the gas.
The short, sharp sound heard when hydrogen burns rapidly at the mouth of the test tube. It is the observation that identifies hydrogen.
A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of the gas. A positive result is that the splint relights.
A wooden splint that has been lit and then blown out, so that the tip still glows red but has no flame. It is inserted into the test tube of gas.
The glowing splint bursts back into flame when it is inserted into the gas. This observation identifies oxygen.
The gas is shaken with, or bubbled through, limewater. A positive result is that the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide. It is the reagent used in the test for carbon dioxide.
The appearance of the limewater after carbon dioxide has been shaken with it or bubbled through it: the clear, colourless solution becomes a milky white, cloudy liquid.
Litmus paper is used. Damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas; a positive result is that the paper is bleached and turns white.
Litmus paper that has been moistened with water before being put into the gas. The specification states that the litmus paper is damp when the test is carried out.
The colour of the litmus paper is removed, so the paper turns white. This is the observation that identifies chlorine.

mcqs.q: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of an unknown gas. Which observation shows that the gas is hydrogen?
options: The splint goes out straight away.
The splint glows brighter and relights.
The gas burns with a steady flame.
The gas burns rapidly with a pop.
mcqs.explain: This is the stated result of the hydrogen test: hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.

mcqs.q: A student has collected a test tube of gas and wants to test whether it is hydrogen. What should the student do?
options: Hold a burning splint at the open end of the test tube.
Insert a glowing splint into the tube of the gas.
Lower a lit splint into the tube and see if it goes out.
Bubble the gas through limewater and look for milkiness.
mcqs.explain: The test for hydrogen uses a burning splint held at the open end of the test tube of gas.

mcqs.q: A student holds a burning splint at the open end of a test tube that should contain hydrogen, but hears no pop. Which is the most likely explanation?
options: Hydrogen does not burn, so no sound is ever produced.
The gas escaped from the tube before the splint was used.
The splint should have been glowing rather than burning.
The test tube was not damp, so the test could not work.
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen only pops if it is still in the tube when the burning splint reaches the open end, so a lost sample gives no sound.

mcqs.q: Which observation shows that a test tube contains oxygen?
options: A burning splint gives a pop in the gas.
The gas burns with a bright flame itself.
A glowing splint relights in the gas.
A glowing splint is put out by the gas.
mcqs.explain: The test for oxygen uses a glowing splint inserted into the gas, and the splint relights.

mcqs.q: A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of oxygen and relights. Which statement about this result is correct?
options: The oxygen lets the splint burn again; the splint is the fuel.
The oxygen itself burns, which is why a flame appears.
The gas is hydrogen, since hydrogen relights a splint.
The splint relights in any gas that is not carbon dioxide.
mcqs.explain: Relighting happens because oxygen supports the combustion of the wooden splint.

mcqs.q: Tube 1 gives a pop when a burning splint is held at its open end. Tube 2 relights a glowing splint. Which gases are in the tubes?
options: Tube 1 hydrogen, tube 2 oxygen
Tube 1 oxygen, tube 2 hydrogen
Both tubes contain hydrogen gas
Tube 1 oxygen, tube 2 chlorine
mcqs.explain: The pop identifies hydrogen and the relighting glowing splint identifies oxygen.

mcqs.q: Which reagent is used in the test for carbon dioxide?
options: An aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide
A solution of solid calcium carbonate
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide
An aqueous solution of calcium chloride
mcqs.explain: Limewater is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide, the reagent named for this test.

mcqs.q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. What is observed?
options: The limewater turns colourless and clear.
The limewater turns from blue to red.
The limewater fizzes and stays colourless.
The limewater turns milky (cloudy).
mcqs.explain: This is the stated positive result for carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: A student shakes a gas sample with limewater in a stoppered tube and the limewater turns milky. Their partner says the test does not count because the gas was not bubbled through. Who is right?
options: The partner: only bubbling through limewater is a valid test.
The partner, because a positive result should leave the limewater clear.
The student, but only if the limewater was made fresh on the same day.
The student, because the gas can be shaken with or bubbled through.
mcqs.explain: The specification allows carbon dioxide to be shaken with limewater or bubbled through it; either way the limewater turns milky.

mcqs.q: Damp litmus paper is put into a test tube of chlorine gas. What is observed?
options: The paper turns red and then stays red.
The paper is bleached and turns white.
The paper changes only if it is dry.
The paper turns blue and then fades.
mcqs.explain: This is the stated result of the chlorine test.

mcqs.q: A student tests a tube of chlorine using dry litmus paper and sees no change. What should the student do next?
options: Record that the gas cannot be chlorine.
Repeat the test using damp litmus paper.
Repeat the test using dry blue litmus paper.
Repeat the test using a glowing splint.
mcqs.explain: The test requires damp litmus paper to be put into the chlorine gas.

mcqs.q: A colourless gas is tested. A burning splint at the open end of the tube goes out with no pop, a glowing splint does not relight, and damp litmus paper put into the gas turns white. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: No conclusion is possible until the test is repeated with dry paper.
The gas is oxygen, because a splint gives no pop in oxygen.
The gas is chlorine, since damp litmus paper is bleached white.
The gas is carbon dioxide, because it put the burning splint out.
mcqs.explain: Bleaching damp litmus paper white is the test result that identifies chlorine, and the two splint tests were both negative.
